title: JESUS SAID, “CALL NO MAN YOUR FATHER.” SO WHY DID PAUL CALL HIMSELF A SPIRITUAL FATHER?
paragraphs: JESUS SAID, “CALL NO MAN YOUR FATHER.” SO WHY DID PAUL CALL HIMSELF A SPIRITUAL FATHER?
One command from Jesus. One startling statement from Paul. And a question that could expose whether we are honoring spiritual leadership—or giving a human being the place that belongs to God alone.
There is a kind of spiritual danger that doesn't begin with rebellion.
Sometimes, it begins with respect.

A young believer walks into a church carrying wounds nobody can see. Perhaps his earthly father abandoned him. Perhaps he grew up without guidance, without affection, without anyone who cared enough to tell him the truth.
Then someone comes along.
A pastor who listens. A mentor who prays. A spiritual leader who opens the Scriptures and helps him understand the Gospel for the first time.
For the first time in years, he feels seen.
He feels protected.
He feels like he belongs.
And one day, with tears in his eyes, he says something that comes straight from his heart.
“You have been like a father to me.”
Beautiful words.
But then someone opens the Bible and reads what Jesus said.
“And call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven.” — Matthew 23:9 (KJV)
Suddenly, the room becomes quiet.
Was that young believer wrong?
Was his gratitude misplaced?
Should Christians never call a pastor, priest, mentor, or spiritual guide their father?
And if Jesus clearly said not to do it, why would the apostle Paul write something that seems to say the opposite?
“For though ye have ten thousand instructors in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel.” — 1 Corinthians 4:15 (KJV)
Read those verses again.
Jesus said, “Call no man your father.”
Paul said, in effect, “I became your father through the Gospel.”
Two statements.
One Bible.
And a question that cannot be answered faithfully by pretending either passage does not exist.
Because this is about far more than a religious title.
It is about authority.
It is about spiritual dependence.
It is about the difference between a shepherd who leads you to Jesus and a leader who slowly teaches you that you cannot reach Jesus without him.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question is not whether you call someone your spiritual father.
Perhaps it is this:

Has someone who was supposed to lead you closer to Christ quietly become the person you are afraid to question, afraid to disappoint, and afraid to leave—even when Scripture tells you something is wrong?
That question deserves an answer.
Not from denominational pride.
Not from tradition alone.
Not from personal resentment toward religious leaders.
But from the Word of God.
To understand what Jesus meant, we must return to the moment He spoke those words.
In Matthew 23, Jesus was confronting the scribes and Pharisees.
He was not delivering a casual lesson about family vocabulary.
He was exposing a religious culture in which outward holiness could conceal inward pride.
He described leaders who loved prominent seats, public recognition, and impressive greetings.
People who wanted to be noticed.
People who enjoyed being treated as spiritually superior.
People who placed burdens on others while failing to practice what they preached.
Then Jesus spoke these piercing words:
“But be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren.” — Matthew 23:8 (KJV)
And immediately afterward:
“And call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven.” — Matthew 23:9 (KJV)
Then:
“Neither be ye called masters: for one is your Master, even Christ.” — Matthew 23:10 (KJV)
And finally, the words that reveal the heart of the entire warning:
“But he that is greatest among you shall be your servant.” — Matthew 23:11 (KJV)
Do you see the movement?
Jesus was confronting the human appetite for spiritual importance.
The desire to stand above others.
The temptation to receive honor that belongs ultimately to God.
He was not merely asking His followers to replace one title with another.
He was dismantling the pride that makes titles dangerous.
And the original Greek helps us see why this matters.
In Matthew 23:9, the word translated “father” is πατέρα (patera), an accusative form of πατήρ (patēr), meaning “father.”
The Greek expression is:
καὶ πατέρα μὴ καλέσητε ὑμῶν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς
Kai patera mē kalesēte hymōn epi tēs gēs.
A close translation is:
“And do not call anyone on earth your father.”
Jesus continues:
εἷς γάρ ἐστιν ὑμῶν ὁ πατὴρ ὁ οὐράνιος
Heis gar estin hymōn ho patēr ho ouranios.
“For one is your Father, the heavenly One.”
Notice something important.
The Greek word itself does not carry a special hidden meaning that magically resolves the difficulty.
Patēr is an ordinary Greek word for father. Its meaning must be understood within the sentence, the surrounding passage, and the wider teaching of Scripture.
And that wider teaching gives us something remarkable.
Jesus Himself used the language of earthly fatherhood.
In Matthew 15:4, He affirmed God's command to honor one's father and mother.
In Matthew 19:19, He repeated the commandment.
In Luke 15, He told the unforgettable parable of a son returning to his father.
And in Matthew 23:30, within the very chapter containing His warning, Jesus referred to the ancestors of His opponents as their fathers.
Therefore, Matthew 23:9 cannot reasonably mean that every use of the word “father” for a human being is sinful.
If it did, the Scriptures themselves would repeatedly violate the supposed rule.
But this does not mean we can dismiss Jesus' command.
Quite the opposite.
Jesus was forbidding something deeper than a word: the elevation of human religious authority into a position that competes with the unique fatherhood of God.
That is the heart of the warning.
And that warning is terrifyingly relevant.
Because spiritual authority can become an idol without ever looking like one.
It may begin with admiration.
Then admiration becomes unquestioning loyalty.
Then loyalty becomes fear.
Then fear becomes silence.
A believer notices something wrong but refuses to speak.
A leader teaches something questionable, but nobody dares examine it.
Someone is wounded, manipulated, or humiliated, yet is told that questioning the leader means dishonoring God.
Eventually, the name of Jesus is still spoken.
The Bible is still opened.
Worship songs are still sung.
But the practical center of the community has shifted.
Everything revolves around one human personality.
And the people are no longer being taught to stand firmly in Christ.
They are being taught to stand only as long as that leader approves.
Friend, that is not spiritual fatherhood as the New Testament presents it.
That is spiritual control.
And Jesus did not shed His blood to rescue sinners from bondage only for religious leaders to place them under another form of bondage.
But now we must face Paul's words.
Because Paul did not simply tolerate spiritual fatherhood as a metaphor.
He used the language personally.
“For in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel.” — 1 Corinthians 4:15 (KJV)
In the original Greek, Paul writes:
ἐν γὰρ Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ διὰ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου ἐγὼ ὑμᾶς ἐγέννησα
En gar Christō Iēsou dia tou euangeliou egō hymas egennēsa.
A close translation is:
“For in Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, I became your father.”
The verb ἐγέννησα (egennēsa) comes from γεννάω (gennaō), meaning to beget, give birth to, or become the parent of someone.
Paul was describing a genuine spiritual relationship.
He had preached the Gospel to the Corinthians.
Through that Gospel ministry, they had come to faith in Christ.
He had labored for their spiritual formation.
He had corrected them.
He had warned them.
He had loved them enough to confront their sins.
But notice the two expressions Paul placed around his claim.
“In Christ Jesus.”
“Through the gospel.”
Those words change everything.
Paul did not claim that he possessed independent spiritual power to produce eternal life.
He did not claim to replace God as their heavenly Father.
He did not claim that the Corinthians belonged to him as personal property.
Their new life came through Christ and the Gospel.
Paul was the human servant through whom that message reached them.
In fact, Paul had already explained this distinction earlier in the same letter.
“Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos, but ministers by whom ye believed, even as the Lord gave to every man?” — 1 Corinthians 3:5 (KJV)
Then he declared:
“I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.” — 1 Corinthians 3:6 (KJV)
And listen to this:
“So then neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase.” — 1 Corinthians 3:7 (KJV)
There it is.
The same apostle who described himself as a spiritual father also insisted that the human minister is nothing in comparison with the God who gives growth.
Paul did not build his ministry around making people dependent on Paul.
He wanted people rooted in Jesus.
That distinction is not small.
It is everything.
Because a true spiritual father does not compete with the heavenly Father.
He serves under Him.
A true spiritual mentor does not replace the Savior.
He points to Him.
A faithful pastor does not make himself the source of grace.
He proclaims the grace that comes through Jesus Christ.
And Paul demonstrated that distinction even when it cost him personal influence.
When believers began dividing themselves around favorite leaders, saying, “I am of Paul” or “I am of Apollos,” Paul confronted their factionalism.
He asked:
“Is Christ divided? was Paul crucified for you? or were ye baptized in the name of Paul?” — 1 Corinthians 1:13 (KJV)
Think about that.
Paul refused to allow the people he had helped bring to Christ to turn his name into the center of their faith.
He could acknowledge a fatherlike relationship without accepting the worshipful loyalty that belongs to Jesus.
That is what healthy spiritual leadership looks like.
And it is why a careful reading of Matthew 23:9 and 1 Corinthians 4:15 does not require us to accuse either Jesus or Paul of contradiction.
Jesus condemns the pride and spiritual supremacy that displace God.
Paul describes a Gospel-centered, fatherlike ministry that remains entirely dependent upon God.
Still, we should not pretend every Christian tradition reaches exactly the same conclusion about religious titles.

Some Christians, including many Catholics and Orthodox believers, understand Paul's words and the broader biblical use of fatherhood language as permitting respectful spiritual titles such as “Father,” provided those titles never rival God's authority.

Other Christians, especially within certain Protestant traditions, avoid addressing ministers as “Father” because they believe the most faithful application of Matthew 23:9 is to reserve that religious form of address for God.
Both positions must take Jesus' warning seriously.
And both should be examined with Scripture rather than caricature.

The New Testament clearly uses fatherhood language for human relationships, including spiritual ones. But that does not, by itself, settle every question about formal clerical titles, institutional authority, or church tradition.
A description of Paul's relationship to the Corinthians is not automatically a command requiring every Christian to address a minister as “Father.”
And Jesus' warning cannot simply be erased because Paul used a fatherhood metaphor.
Faithfulness requires us to hold both truths together.
The Bible recognizes fatherlike spiritual care while warning against the exaltation of human religious authority.
But there is another passage that makes this even more personal.
Paul wrote to the Thessalonians:
“As ye know how we exhorted and comforted and charged every one of you, as a father doth his children.” — 1 Thessalonians 2:11 (KJV)
What did fatherlike ministry look like to Paul?
Exhortation.
Comfort.
Encouragement.
Personal care.
A call to walk worthy of God.
And in the same chapter, Paul also described his ministry using the tenderness of a nursing mother caring for her children.
His point was not status.
His point was sacrificial love.
He was willing to give not only the Gospel but his own life in service to those he loved.
Now compare that with the kind of leadership Jesus condemned.
One seeks the highest seat.
The other bends down to serve.
One wants people to notice his greatness.
The other wants people to know the greatness of Christ.
One uses spiritual authority to make people smaller.
The other uses spiritual responsibility to help believers grow into maturity.
And perhaps this is where the question stops being theological theory and begins touching the hidden places of our lives.
Because some of us know what it means to long for a father.
Maybe your earthly father was present physically but absent emotionally.
Maybe he provided food but never affection.
Maybe he gave correction without encouragement.
Maybe the word “father” does not bring comfort to your mind.
It brings pain.
And when a pastor or mentor finally showed you patience, compassion, and consistent care, something inside you began to heal.
There is nothing shameful about being grateful for someone God used to help you.
Spiritual mentorship can be a beautiful gift.
But even the most loving spiritual mentor is still human.
He can become tired.
He can misunderstand.
He can sin.
He can fail.
He may even disappoint you deeply.
And if your entire faith rests upon his perfection, what happens when his humanity becomes impossible to ignore?
What happens when the voice you trusted says something that contradicts Scripture?
What happens when the person who taught you about grace fails to show grace?
What happens when the shepherd himself needs repentance?
This is why your relationship with God must never be reduced to your relationship with a religious leader.
The man who introduced you to Jesus is not the Jesus who saved you.
Read that again.
The person who prayed with you did not die for your sins.
The person who baptized you did not rise from the grave for your justification.
The person who taught you the Bible is not the eternal Word made flesh.
And the person who helped you find your way home is not the Father waiting to receive you.
There is only one Savior.
“For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.” — 1 Timothy 2:5 (KJV)
One mediator.
Jesus Christ.
This does not eliminate the importance of pastors, teachers, elders, or spiritual mentors.
Ephesians 4:11–13 describes Christ giving ministry leaders to equip the saints and build up the body of Christ.
Hebrews 13:17 teaches believers to take spiritual leadership seriously, while reminding us that leaders must give an account.
And 1 Peter 5:2–3 commands elders to shepherd God's flock willingly, not as domineering rulers, but as examples.
Biblical leadership is real.
Biblical accountability is real.
Biblical submission has a place.
But none of those truths gives any leader permission to demand unquestioning obedience, conceal wrongdoing, or claim the authority that belongs to Christ alone.
Even the apostle Peter, when writing to fellow elders, did not present himself as a supreme personality beyond correction.
He directed attention to the Chief Shepherd.
And that title belongs to Jesus.
So how can you recognize a spiritually healthy mentor?
Watch what happens when you ask a sincere biblical question.
Does he patiently open the Scriptures, or does he treat your question as personal betrayal?
Watch what happens when he makes a mistake.
Does he repent, or does he insist that his position places him beyond accountability?
Watch what happens when you begin growing spiritually.
Does he rejoice as you become more grounded in Christ, or does he become threatened when you no longer depend on his approval?
Watch what happens when people praise him.
Does he receive gratitude with humility and direct glory toward God, or does he cultivate an atmosphere where his name matters more than the name of Jesus?
These are not perfect tests of a person's heart.
Only God sees the heart completely.
But they are important questions about observable fruit.
Jesus said:
“Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.” — Matthew 7:20 (KJV)
And the fruit of faithful ministry should not be spiritual captivity.
It should be growing faith, truth, holiness, love, humility, and maturity in Christ.
That is why the apostle John could write:
Notice what brings joy.
Not that his spiritual children repeat his name.
Not that they defend his reputation at any cost.
Not that they become incapable of thinking without his permission.
But that they walk in truth.
And Jesus Christ is the truth.
Now, before anyone uses this article as an excuse to despise pastors, mock priests, reject spiritual counsel, or become unteachable, we need to confront another danger.
Pride does not exist only in religious leaders.
It can also live in the hearts of those who refuse to be led.
Some people say, “I follow Jesus, not men,” but use those words to escape every form of correction.
They reject accountability.
They dismiss faithful teaching.
They confuse independence with spiritual maturity.
That is not what Jesus taught either.
The same Lord who warned against religious pride also gave His Church shepherds and teachers.
The same New Testament that warns against domineering leaders calls believers to humility, mutual service, and fellowship.
The answer to abusive authority is not the rejection of all authority.
The answer is authority submitted to Christ.
The answer to spiritual manipulation is not spiritual isolation.
The answer is truth, accountability, and relationships shaped by the Gospel.
And the answer to a leader who has taken too much space in your heart is not necessarily hatred toward that leader.
It may begin with repentance.
Not only his.
Yours, too, if you have given a human being the trust, fear, or devotion that belongs to God.
Because idolatry is not always a statue.
Sometimes it is a person whose approval we fear losing more than we fear disobeying God.
Sometimes it is a ministry we refuse to examine.
Sometimes it is a religious title we treat as proof of holiness.
Sometimes it is our own reputation as a loyal follower.
And Jesus loves us too much to leave those idols untouched.
He did not come to create a new class of untouchable religious celebrities.
He came to reconcile sinners to the Father.
He came to seek and save the lost.
He came to expose hypocrisy and offer mercy to the repentant.
He came to bear the sins of people who had trusted the wrong things, followed the wrong voices, and wandered far from God.
At the cross, the Son of God did not merely teach us humility.
He demonstrated it.
The One who possessed all authority allowed Himself to be mocked.
The One who deserved every crown wore a crown of thorns.
The One before whom every knee will bow knelt in service and gave Himself for sinners.
And when He rose from the grave, He did not become one spiritual guide among many.
He stood revealed as the victorious Lord and Savior.
That is the difference between Christianity and a personality cult.
Christianity does not end with a human leader.
It begins and ends with Jesus Christ.
And this is where our Gospel Warrior theme becomes more than a beautiful phrase.
Think of Peter.
He had promised loyalty.
He had declared that even if everyone else abandoned Jesus, he would remain faithful.
But when the pressure came, he denied knowing the Lord.
Three times.
The man who had spoken so boldly broke under fear.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine remembering the sound of your own voice denying the Savior you loved.
Imagine wondering whether your failure had permanently destroyed your calling.
But after the resurrection, Jesus met Peter in his brokenness.
In John 21, Jesus restored him and entrusted him with a responsibility:
“Feed my sheep.” — John 21:17 (KJV)
Not “Build a kingdom around your personality.”
Not “Make people dependent on your greatness.”
Not “Convince everyone that you are incapable of failure.”
Feed My sheep.
Whose sheep?
Jesus' sheep.
That one word matters.
My.
The flock belongs to Christ.
The Church belongs to Christ.
The redeemed belong to Christ.
Even the most faithful shepherd is only a servant caring for what belongs to Another.
And perhaps that is the word some leaders desperately need to hear.
You do not have to pretend you are the source of everyone's spiritual life.
You do not have to be the answer to every question.
You do not have to control every decision.
You do not have to make people afraid of leaving your ministry.
You are called to serve faithfully, teach truthfully, love sacrificially, and point people to the Chief Shepherd.
And perhaps that is also the word some wounded believers need to hear.
You can honor the person who helped you without surrendering your conscience.
You can appreciate a mentor without making him infallible.
You can receive correction without accepting manipulation.
You can forgive someone without pretending that harm never happened.
You can seek wise pastoral care while remembering that your ultimate hope rests in Christ.
And if a leader has wounded you, that wound does not mean Jesus has abandoned you.
Human shepherds can fail.
The Chief Shepherd remains faithful.
Now return to the original question.
Should Christians call anyone on earth their spiritual father when Jesus said, “Call no man your father”?
Here is the most biblically responsible answer I can give.

Scripture permits fatherhood language to describe genuine spiritual care, as Paul himself demonstrates. But Scripture never permits a human spiritual father to take the unique place of God, claim unquestionable spiritual supremacy, or become a rival to Christ.

Whether a Christian should use “Father” as a formal religious title remains a matter on which traditions disagree. Those who use it must not empty Matthew 23:9 of its force. Those who avoid it must not ignore Paul's fatherhood language.
No one should be pressured to violate a sincerely held, Scripture-informed conviction about such a title.
And every Christian, regardless of denomination, must face the warning Jesus gave.
Because a person can refuse the title “Father” and still idolize a pastor.
A person can use the title “Father” respectfully while genuinely recognizing God as the supreme Father.
The title alone does not reveal the whole condition of the heart.
But the way authority is exercised, the way Scripture is handled, and the way Christ is honored reveal a great deal.
And that brings us to something we cannot afford to overlook.
The most dangerous spiritual father is not necessarily the one who accepts the title. It is the one who demands the place that belongs to God.
And the safest spiritual mentor is not necessarily the one who refuses every title.
It is the one who continually leads you away from dependence on himself and toward deeper dependence on Jesus.
That is the kind of discipleship worth building.
That is the kind of truth worth defending.
That is the kind of Gospel-centered community Gospel Warrior exists to encourage.
Not a community where people worship a personality.
Not a community where questions are silenced.
Not a community where religious titles become weapons.

But a community where Scripture is examined carefully, Christ is exalted faithfully, sinners are called to repentance, wounded believers find biblical encouragement, and spiritual growth becomes a lifelong pursuit.
And if this message has challenged you, please do not simply move on to the next post.
Ask yourself one question.
Am I following Jesus through the help of faithful spiritual leaders, or have I allowed a human leader to become the center of my faith?
That question may reveal something painful.
But the grace of God is not afraid of exposing what needs to change.
You do not need to reveal private wounds publicly to prove your faith. A simple prayer, an honest question, or a testimony of God's faithfulness can become a blessing to someone else.
Not to win an argument.
Not to attack a denomination.
Not to embarrass a pastor or priest.
But because someone in your circle may be silently wrestling with this very question.
Someone may be confusing spiritual loyalty with spiritual bondage.
Someone may be rejecting every form of Christian mentorship because one leader betrayed their trust.
Someone may need to discover that honoring faithful spiritual care and worshiping God alone are not enemies.
There is also a deeper way to help this ministry continue.
Gospel Warrior is committed to making biblical teaching, Christian reading, and discipleship resources more accessible to people who are hungry for the Word of God.
And here is something important.
We believe the Gospel should never be treated as merchandise.
God's grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation is not reserved for paying supporters.
The Word of God is not a luxury that belongs only to those who can afford it.
That is precisely why freely accessible Christian resources matter.
Scripture says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
Not guilt.
Not fear.
But a willing heart that wants to help good work continue.
These items are not the reason we preach Christ.
You are no less valuable.
Your prayers matter.
Your thoughtful comments matter.
Your sharing matters.
Your willingness to help another person understand the Gospel matters.
We want them to encounter more than religious content.
We want them to encounter the truth of Scripture and the saving message of Jesus Christ.
And before you leave, remember the words of Jesus:
“And all ye are brethren.” — Matthew 23:8 (KJV)
What a beautiful reminder.
In a world obsessed with titles, positions, recognition, and power, Jesus called His followers to remember their shared dependence on God.
The pastor needs grace.
The priest needs grace.
The teacher needs grace.
The mentor needs grace.
The new believer needs grace.
The person who has failed needs grace.
And the person who thinks he has never failed needs grace more than he realizes.
None of us stands before God because a human spiritual father has made us worthy.
We stand only through the mercy of Jesus Christ.
The One who bore our sins.
The One who conquered the grave.
The One who calls us to repentance and faith.
The One who gives us access to the Father.
So honor those who have faithfully taught you.
Pray for those entrusted with spiritual responsibility.
Be willing to receive biblical correction.
Refuse to turn human servants into spiritual idols.
And never forget whose blood purchased your redemption.
Because when every earthly title fades, when every human reputation is forgotten, and when every earthly ministry has completed its work, one name will remain above every name.
Jesus Christ.
And if your spiritual father truly loves you, he will want you to remember that long after you have forgotten his own name.
The hands that helped lead you to Jesus may one day let you down—but the nail-scarred hands of Jesus will never lose their power to save.
